newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Aid no substitute for political action - ECHO boss.
newsitem.headline: Aid no substitute for political action - ECHO boss.

text.p: EU relief aid to the Great Lakes is no substitute for a political solution to the crisis, the new head of the European Community Humanitarian Office (ECHO) told the European Parliament on Wednesday.

Alberto Navarro, who took over as director of ECHO this month, told the European Parliament's development committee that the troubled region would continue to receive the lion's share of EU emergency relief aid in 1997.
But humanitarian aid could never be a substitute for timely action to prevent disasters like the Rwandan genocide and the subsequent refugee crisis.

"Failure to find political solutions to problems is something that ECHO and the humanitarian community cannot offset," he said. "We cannot be used as an alibi for politicians who have to find political solutions."
After Rwanda, Burundi and Eastern Zaire, relief operations in the former Yugoslavia and the Caucasus were ECHO's next priorities, Navarro said.
ECHO would also continue to supply aid to children and women in Afghanistan, who were "enduring ghastly problems" under the fundamentalist rule of the Taliban.

Faced with questions from MEPs about the criticism levelled at his recently created department, Navarro said ECHO was trying to tackle massive humanitarian problems -- starvation, disease, conflicts and natural disasters, refugee crises -- with limited staff and resources.
ECHO's budget for 1997 was 650 million Ecus -- equivalent to only two percent of what the European Union plans to spend on the common agriculture policy, he stressed.
Some non-governmental relief organisations (NGOs) have said ECHO is too rigid and unwieldy for them to work with in emergency situations, though about 170 have long-term standard contracts with ECHO.

Navarro agreed it was important to be flexible enough to respond to disasters swiftly but said it was also vital for ECHO to have rules which guaranteed that any NGOs it funded were open, efficient and trustworthy.

The outspoken humanitarian aid commissioner, Emma Bonino, who has repeatedly voiced her exasperation at the time the West has taken to respond to the Great Lakes crisis, was completing a study on ECHO operations which could recommend improvements in the way it functions, Navarro said.
The report is also expected to recommend proper coordination between the member states and ECHO, who between them fund 50 percent of all humanitarian aid.
Everyone paid lip service to ccordination but this had not really been translated into action, Navarro said.
He said it was also difficult to put into practice the principle of closely involving local people in relief operations, seen as an important factor in diffusing conflict.
In some respects, humanitarian aid was a minefield. For example, ECHO needed to look more closely in future at the effect of its food aid operations.
MEPs were concerned that EU taxpayers were having to compensate European farmers for surplus produce, which was then sent to developing countries as food aid.
Unless managed carefully, these shipments could flood local markets and force down food prices, harming local producers, Navarro said.
The new ECHO boss skirted round criticism from MEPs that in spite of its limited funds ECHO appeared to be spending too much money on glossy publicity.
EU taxpayers needed to see their money was being well speent, he said.
